## 1. Traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1:** On the same day as the "blasphemy" accusation and his family's visit, Jesus leaves what was probably Peter's house in Capernaum. Opposition is growing and popularity is falling, so this is a turning point, and parables now begin. (Precept Austin)
- Ellicott thinks the Pharisees' hostility helped prompt the new parable method. It was harder to attack and tested people's character. (Ellicott)
- Gill suggests Jesus may have left because the house couldn't hold the crowd, or to rest. (Gill)

**v. 2:** The boat kept Him clear of the crush and let Him be seen and heard. (Gill; EW)
- Sitting was the normal teaching position for a rabbi and signals authoritative teaching. (Precept Austin; Gill)
- Ellicott adds that the boat put a little water between Jesus and a possibly hostile crowd. (Ellicott)
- Chrysostom: He sat so He could face everyone, "fishing" for those on land. (Chrysostom)

**v. 3:** This is the first time Matthew uses "parable." The word means "thrown alongside," a comparison. (Precept Austin; Ellicott; EW)
- EW, quoting Barclay, warns against turning parables into allegories where every detail means something. (EW)
- Precept Austin argues "parable of the soils" is a better name, because the sower and seed stay the same and only the soil changes. (Precept Austin; MacArthur makes the same point: https://www.gty.org/library/blog/B170809/the-parable-of-the-sower-and-bad-evangelism)
- Who is the sower?
  - Gill: Christ first, and in a lesser sense every minister. (Gill)
  - Chrysostom: Christ "went out" by taking on flesh. (Chrysostom)
  - Spurgeon: the preacher sows seed he didn't make. (https://www.spurgeon.org/resource-library/sermons/the-parable-of-the-sower/)

**v. 4:** The path was hard, beaten ground where seed stayed on top for the birds. (Ellicott; EW)
- Gill reads the birds as devils, the "power of the air." (Gill)
- Chrysostom notes the text says the seed "fell," not that He threw it there. (Chrysostom)
- Wesley: Jesus lists the hindrances in the order they happen. (Wesley)

**v. 5:** Rocky ground is probably a thin layer of soil over rock. The quick growth comes from the same cause that later kills it. (Ellicott; EW)
- Gill: these are hearers with slight convictions and a show of grace but "no real heart work." (Gill)

**v. 6:** Growth was too fast, and the rock underneath made the heat worse. (Ellicott)
- Chrysostom: the plant died for lack of root, not because of the heat. (Chrysostom)

**v. 7:** The thorn roots were already under the surface and grew up alongside the grain. The grain wasn't killed suddenly but slowly strangled. (Ellicott)
- EW: this is fertile soil, perhaps too fertile. (EW)

**v. 8:** A hundredfold was rare but not unheard of; Isaac's harvest in Genesis 26:12 is cited. (Ellicott; Gill)
- Gill: the yields are different amounts of the same grace in believers. (Gill)
- Wesley defines good soil as soft, deep and cleared of thorns. (Wesley)
- Chrysostom: only one part in four is saved, and even good soil varies. (Chrysostom)

**v. 9:** EW says this is not a call for everyone to listen. It is a call for the spiritually sensitive to pay special attention. (EW)
- Gill: it is meant to make people want to understand. (Gill)
- Ellicott: perhaps a formula from the rabbinic schools. (Ellicott)

**v. 10:** The disciples, probably in the boat, asked out of the crowd's hearing. (Ellicott)
- Gill: they asked partly because they didn't understand either. (Gill)

**v. 11:** A "mystery" isn't something impossible to understand. It is a secret now revealed to insiders. (Ellicott)
- Several commentators on Bible Hub's combined page say the same: things only revealed under the gospel. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/13-11.htm)

**v. 12:** Ellicott calls it a proverb about spiritual growth, close to the parables of the talents and pounds. (Ellicott)
- EW, quoting Barclay: life is always gaining more or losing more. (EW)

**v. 13:** EW: the parables were a mercy to the hardened, so they wouldn't pile up more judgment. (EW)
- Ellicott: they are mainly a judgment (compare Mark and Luke, "so that"), but with mercy in them, since a parable might still start people thinking. (Ellicott)

**v. 14:** Ellicott: the Greek means complete fulfilment that is still going on. The verse is also quoted in John 12 and Acts 28. (Ellicott)
- Gill: the blindness continued until Judea was destroyed. (Gill)

**v. 15:** This is willful ignorance that refuses to look in case it leads to conversion. (Ellicott)
- EW, quoting Trapp: "dull" literally means a "fat" heart. (EW)

**v. 16:** The disciples saw dimly, but they had eyes that wanted light. (Ellicott)
- Wesley: they value the light they're given. (Wesley)

**v. 17:** The prophets were "men of desires" who saw the kingdom from far off. Ellicott squares this with John 8:56. (Ellicott)
- EW, quoting Spurgeon: the shortest summer day is longer than the longest winter day. (EW)

**v. 18:** The "you" is emphatic: the meaning held back from others is given to you. (Ellicott)

**v. 19:** Not understanding is a moral failure more than an intellectual one. Ellicott links the "evil one" to the Lord's Prayer. (Ellicott)
- EW links it to 2 Corinthians 4:4: Satan works to keep people in the dark about the gospel. (EW)
- Wesley: the evil one works inwardly through distracting thoughts, or through people who change the subject. (Wesley)
- Calvin: like hungry birds, Satan grabs the word before it can sprout. (https://www.ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom32.ii.xix.html)

**v. 20:** Ellicott says excitement-driven settings, such as revival meetings, produce more of these quick conversions. (Ellicott)
- EW, quoting Spurgeon: the problem was lack of depth, not that the conversion was sudden. (EW)

**v. 21:** "Root" is conviction that reaches reason, conscience and will. (Ellicott)
- EW, quoting France: "falls away" means being tripped up, a collapse under pressure. (EW)
- Chrysostom: these fall through weakness, not carelessness. (Chrysostom)

**v. 22:** The problem is a divided heart. Ellicott says "worries" is the same word as "take no thought" in Matthew 6. (Ellicott)
- Chrysostom: the trouble is "the deceitfulness of riches," not riches themselves; a person can be rich without being deceived. (Chrysostom)
- Wesley: worries are thorns for the poor, and wealth is the thorn for the rich. (Wesley)

**v. 23:** "Understands" means taking the word in, not just grasping it intellectually. (Ellicott)
- Ellicott also says the soils are not fixed: they can be improved, and preachers should prepare the ground (Jeremiah 4:3). (Ellicott)
- Chrysostom and Precept Austin (quoting Steven Cole) agree the soils can change. (Chrysostom; Precept Austin)
- EW: each of us is sometimes like all four soils. (EW)

**v. 24:** The parable is spoken to the crowd again. (Ellicott)
- Wesley: here the kingdom means the gospel age, and Christ sows only good seed. (Wesley)

**v. 25:** Wesley: the servants should have stayed awake; the Lord doesn't sleep. The weed is darnel, which looks like wheat. (Wesley)
- EW, quoting France: darnel is poisonous and almost impossible to tell from wheat until the heads form. (EW)
- Calvin's snippet says that asking why the devil sows "while Christ is asleep" is over-reading the detail. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/matthew-13.html)

**v. 26:** Darnel rarely shows at first; at first everything looks like peace and joy. (Wesley)

**v. 27:** The weeds are "not from the parent of good." (Wesley)

**v. 28:** Wesley sees here a plain answer to where evil comes from: God made free creatures, and an enemy did this, with human cooperation. (Wesley)
- EW: this describes corruption inside the community of God's people that can look genuine. (EW)

**v. 29:** The separation waits for the harvest to protect the wheat. (EW)
- EW, quoting Carson: this answers whether the Messiah's people should separate immediately, and the answer is no. (EW)

## 2. Where Protestant traditions differ

**vv. 11–13, why some understand and others don't:**
- Gill [Baptist]: knowledge is given by God's sovereign will to the elect. "Them" means those not among the elect, and Jesus' preaching method followed that decree. (Gill)
- Calvin [Reformed]: Jesus doesn't put the blame on them here. He uses it to praise the grace given to the apostles, because it isn't given equally to all. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/matthew-13.html)
- Spurgeon [Baptist]: they deadened their own faculties. When God passes someone by, it is because of their sin; when He chooses someone, it isn't because they are better. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-13-commentary-spurgeon)
- Wesley [Methodist]: "has" means *makes use of* grace. That is God's fixed rule. It is never God's will that hinders, only people's "voluntary perverseness." (Wesley)

**vv. 20–22, were the failed hearers ever truly changed?**
- Gill: the rocky ground shows only a show of grace. (Gill)
- Wesley: the joy came from "preventing grace," but there was no deep work. The thorny-ground hearer, though, was "in a great measure inwardly changed" and yet still choked into unfruitfulness. (Wesley)

**v. 23, what made the soil good?**
- Spurgeon: not good by nature but made good by grace. (https://www.spurgeon.org/resource-library/sermons/the-parable-of-the-sower/)
- Gill: made good by the Spirit. (Gill)
- Ellicott: says the parable raises the question but doesn't answer it, and mentions "prevenient grace." (Ellicott)

**vv. 28–29, church discipline:**
- Wesley: darnel means Christians who have the outward form without the power. Open sinners are thistles and should be put out of the church "without delay." (Wesley)

## 3. Other views (only Chrysostom found)
- **vv. 3–8:** The sower sows on every kind of ground without favouring anyone, so no one can blame Him. (Chrysostom, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/200144.htm)
- **vv. 19–22:** The blame lies with the soil's choice, not its nature. "It rests with us" whether the seed is taken away. (Chrysostom)
- **v. 23:** The different yields show God's mercy: He doesn't demand one single level of virtue. (Chrysostom)
